Rule 110 fails this for all W > 5 (e.g., W=6 has a transient/cycle structure exceeding 2). The structural property separating these pairs is additive linearity (Rule 90 is XOR-linear; Rule 184's particle dynamics map to a linear ballot problem conservation law), which guarantees the phase space is a disjoint union of cycles (no long transients) and limits maximal cycle periods to powers of 2 (bounded by 2^W, but strictly \u2264 2 for small W), whereas nonlinear rules like 110 possess gliders/particles that interact chaotically to create unbounded transients. Rule 54 is predicted to FAIL this property for all W because it exhibits nonlinear glider interactions similar to Rule 110, producing long transients.","counterconditions":[{"case":"Rule 110 unexpectedly settles into a global homogeneous state for all W <= 11, making all cycles length 1.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"Rule 184 possesses a chaotic attractor of length > 2 for W=9 due to an unforeseen boundary resonance.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"Rule 90's cycle length is strictly 1 (not 2) for all W in [5,11], invalidating the structural necessity of the 'length 2' bound.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"Rule 54 is discovered to be perfectly additive over GF(2) in a way previously unrecognized, bounding its cycle length to 2.","eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Rule 90 is an additive cellular automaton governed by XOR over a finite vector space GF(2)^W. Rule 184 is a traffic model where particles (1s) move right; its dynamics are isomorphic to a solvable ballot problem, mapping to a linear permutation of spacetime diagonals, fundamentally constraining its state space to short cycles and immediate transients. Rule 110 is Turing complete; its nonlinear local rule generates interacting localized structures (gliders). These gliders undergo elastic and inelastic collisions, taking O(W^2) steps to resolve into periodic background, easily exceeding 4*W steps and yielding complex attractors of length > 2.
